desc: The core software that manages hardware and provides services to applications.
A text-based interface for entering commands, as opposed to a GUI.
A visual, window-and-icon based interface.
The free-software project/collection of tools that forms much of a Linux userland.
Software whose source is freely available to view, modify, and redistribute.
A copyleft open-source license requiring derivative works to also be open-sourced.
The structure used to organize and store files on a storage device.
The standard that defines directory purposes, e.g. /etc, /var, /opt.
A layer that pools physical storage into volume groups and resizable logical volumes.
A disk or partition initialized for use by LVM.
A pool of one or more physical volumes that LVM allocates logical volumes from.
A resizable virtual partition carved out of a volume group.
The fixed-size allocation unit LVM uses to divide a physical volume.
Combines multiple disks for redundancy and/or performance (e.g. RAID 0, 1, 5, 10).
The standard disk-encryption specification used by cryptsetup on Linux.
Fine-grained file permissions beyond the standard owner/group/other model, set with setfacl/getfacl.
A unique ID assigned to a filesystem/partition, often used in /etc/fstab instead of a device path.
A protocol for sharing directories over a network so remote hosts can mount them locally.
The Windows-native file/printer sharing protocol; Samba implements it on Linux.
A dialect of SMB used for network file sharing.
Delivers block-level storage over a standard IP network.
A high-performance journaling filesystem, the RHEL/CentOS default for many years.
The numeric identifier assigned to a user account.
The numeric identifier assigned to a group.
A permission bit that runs an executable with the file owner's privileges.
A permission bit that runs an executable with the group's privileges, or makes new files in a directory inherit its group.
A modular framework Linux uses for authentication, including account lockout modules like pam_tally2/pam_faillock.
A protocol for querying and maintaining centralized directory (user/group) information.
Manages access to remote identity/authentication providers such as LDAP and AD.
Microsoft's directory service, sometimes joined by Linux hosts for centralized auth.
The core protocol for addressing and routing packets across networks.
A connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol.
A connectionless, low-overhead transport protocol without delivery guarantees.
Resolves hostnames to IP addresses (and vice versa).
Automatically assigns IP addresses and network settings to hosts.
An encrypted protocol for remote shell access and file transfer (scp/sftp).
An older, unencrypted protocol for transferring files.
File transfer carried over an encrypted SSH connection.
The protocol used to transfer web content.
HTTP encrypted with TLS/SSL.
The modern protocol for encrypting network connections; the successor to SSL.
The older, now-deprecated predecessor to TLS.
Rewrites source/destination addresses so private-network hosts can share a public IP.
An encrypted tunnel that extends a private network across a public one.
Segments a physical network into isolated logical broadcast domains.
The largest packet size a network link will carry without fragmentation.
Resolves an IP address to a MAC address on a local network segment.
Carries diagnostic/error messages, e.g. ping and traceroute.
Synchronizes system clocks over a network.
The protocol used to send email between mail servers.
The hardware address burned into (or spoofed on) a network interface.
The hardware (or virtual) adapter that connects a host to a network.
A complete hostname including its domain, e.g. host.example.com.
A mandatory access control system using labeled contexts, with modes Enforcing/Permissive/Disabled.
The traditional owner/group/other permission model, where the owner controls access -- contrast with MAC (Mandatory Access Control), where policy like SELinux decides access instead.
An implementation of OpenPGP used for encrypting data and signing/verifying files or packages.
The system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities used to manage trust.
An entity that issues and signs digital certificates.
A request submitted to a CA to obtain a signed certificate.
Authentication requiring two or more independent proof factors.
MFA using exactly two factors, e.g. a password plus a one-time code.
A one-time code that changes on a time interval, common in MFA apps.
Monitors traffic/logs and alerts on suspicious activity without blocking it.
Like an IDS, but can actively block detected threats.
A standardized identifier for a publicly known security vulnerability.
Aggregates and correlates logs/events for security monitoring.
The numeric identifier the kernel assigns to a running process.
The PID of the process that started a given process.
The modern init system managing services (units), targets, and boot on most distros.
The older init system using numbered /etc/rc scripts, largely replaced by systemd.
The classic daemon/table for scheduling recurring jobs via crontab.
The package format and tool used on Red Hat-family distributions.
The package format used on Debian/Ubuntu-family distributions.
The RPM-based package manager used on older RHEL/CentOS releases.
The modern successor to YUM on current RPM-based distributions.
The front-end package manager for .deb packages on Debian/Ubuntu.
An emulated computer running its own OS on top of a hypervisor.
The Linux kernel's built-in hypervisor/virtualization module.
The standard defining container image and runtime formats used by Docker/Podman.
An OS-level virtualization technology for running isolated Linux systems on one kernel.
A human-readable data format commonly used for config files and automation (e.g. Ansible).
A lightweight structured data format widely used for config and APIs.
A defined interface for programs to interact with a service or system.
Managing/provisioning infrastructure through versioned config files instead of manual steps.
Automated pipelines that build, test, and ship code changes.
The processor that executes instructions.
Volatile working memory used by running processes.
Traditional spinning-platter magnetic storage.
Flash-based storage with no moving parts.
A common standard for connecting peripherals and external storage.
A standard bus for connecting internal expansion hardware.
Legacy firmware that initializes hardware and hands off to the boot loader.
The modern replacement for BIOS, supporting larger disks and Secure Boot.
The most common Linux boot loader, configured via grub.cfg.
The legacy partitioning scheme/boot sector limited to 4 primary partitions and 2TB disks.
The modern partitioning scheme supporting more partitions and disks over 2TB.
Disk space used as overflow when physical RAM is exhausted.
A dedicated file-level storage device accessed over a network.
A dedicated network providing block-level shared storage.
Refers to a terminal device/session, physical or virtual.
Signals that no more data remains to be read from a stream/file.
The default input stream (file descriptor 0) a program reads from.
The default output stream (file descriptor 1) a program writes to.
The default stream (file descriptor 2) for error/diagnostic output.
A pattern-matching syntax used by tools like grep, sed, and awk.
A single chip integrating CPU, memory controller, and other components (common on embedded/IoT devices).
Network-connected embedded devices, often running minimal Linux.
Network traffic prioritization to manage bandwidth and latency.
A network spanning a large geographic area, e.g. connecting sites over the internet.
A network confined to a small area such as a building or office.
The slash notation (e.g. /24) used to express subnet size.
The DNS record defining a zone's primary authoritative info, e.g. refresh/retry timers.
A DNS record used for reverse lookups, resolving an IP back to a hostname.
